gbs333-h47986-d1e102.summary: Places Distinction 23 within the plan of Book III. Having treated Christ the head alone in distinctions 1–22, Lombard now treats the head together with the members with respect to the perfections of virtues, gifts, and grace. These perfections are divided into habits (virtues and gifts) and acts (the precepts, from d. 37). The habits are divided into virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit (d. 34), the virtues into theological and cardinal (d. 33), and the theological into faith, hope (d. 26), and charity (d. 27). (The heading reads 'Distinctio XXII', though this is the preamble to d. 23.)
claims: Distinctions 1–22 of Book III concern Christ the head alone; the following distinctions treat head and members together with respect to virtues, gifts, and grace.
These perfections are treated first as habits (virtues and gifts), then as acts commanded by the precepts (from d. 37).
The theological virtues are treated in order: faith, hope (d. 26), charity (d. 27).

gbs333-h47986-d1e159.summary: Subdivides Lombard's treatment of faith into three parts: faith in itself (habit and act), its object (d. 24), and its subject (d. 25). Distinction 23 treats faith in itself with respect to its substance or quiddity: its definition, its formation, its unity, and its priority. Announces that the distinction's teaching can be abbreviated in three conclusions.
claims: Lombard treats faith in itself, then in its object, then in its subject (d. 25).
Distinction 23 treats the definition, formation, unity, and priority of faith.

gbs333-h47986-d1e190.summary: First conclusion, on the definition and kinds of faith. Faith taken as a habit is the virtue by which things pertaining to religion that are not seen are believed, and, following Hebrews 11, it is the substance of things to be hoped for and the argument of things not apparent. Distinguishes believing God exists (credere Deum), believing God (credere Deo), and believing in God (credere in Deum). The first two are also found in demons and the wicked; believing in God with firm charity belongs only to true Christians.
claims: Faith as a habit is a virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed.
Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for and the argument of things not apparent.
Believing that God exists and believing God belong also to demons and the wicked; believing in God with charity belongs only to true Christians.
concepts: credere Deum / credere Deo / credere in Deum

gbs333-h47986-d1e213.summary: Second conclusion, on the formation of faith. Either of two accounts may be held without danger: that unformed faith passes away when charity arrives, or that it remains and is formed and perfected by the charity that supervenes.
claims: It is safe to hold either that unformed faith passes away at the coming of charity or that it remains and is formed by charity.

gbs333-h47986-d1e226.summary: Third conclusion, on the unity and priority of faith. Although 'faith' is said in many ways, faith is one, not in number but in kind, both in its object and in its habit. It is the first of the virtues in natural order. Notes that Lombard expounds each clause at length in the text.
claims: Faith is one in kind, not in number, both in object and in habit.
Faith is first among the virtues in natural order.
concepts: priority of faith among the virtues

gbs333-h47986.summary: This Praeambulum opens the treatment of the theological virtues in Book III. It places Distinction 23 in Lombard's plan: after Christ the head (dd. 1–22), Lombard treats head and members with respect to virtues, gifts, and grace, starting with faith, then hope and charity. It divides the treatment of faith into faith in itself (d. 23), its object (d. 24), and its subject (d. 25). It then condenses d. 23 into three conclusions. (1) Faith as a habit is a virtue by which unseen religious truths are believed, the substance of things hoped for. Believing in God with charity, unlike believing that God exists or believing God, belongs only to true Christians. (2) It is safe to hold either that unformed faith gives way to charity or that charity forms it. (3) Faith is one in kind, not in number, and first among the virtues in natural order.
claims: Book III, from d. 23, treats the virtues, gifts, and precepts as perfections of Christ and his members, beginning with the theological virtues.
Faith is treated in itself (d. 23), in its object (d. 24), and in its subject (d. 25).
Faith as a habit is the virtue by which unseen things of religion are believed; believing in God with charity is proper to true Christians.
Either account of the relation of unformed faith to charity may be held without danger.
Faith is specifically, not numerically, one and is first of the virtues in natural order.
